short: The name Mauri comes from the Mauritanian or Moorish people, the native population of Mauretania, which is in Northwest Africa. The Mauri by Strabo, who wrote in the early 1st century, is a local name that was also adopted in Latin, while he cites the same nation's Greek name as the Mauretania. The name Mauri as a tribal confederation or common ethnic designation probably therefore corresponds roughly to the people known in earlier history as the Numidians. There is also a theory that by this time the given title, used in the Roman army, did not designate an ethnicity but a particular type of military unit, but what type of unit, we can only speculate. Equites - a new type of cavalry appeared in the 3rd century (probably under Diocletian), has nothing in common with the ancient Roman class of Equites (cavalrymen) or legionary cavalry of the Principate period (equites legionis). Literally translated from Latin as «horsemen», it is a cavalry unit of any type.
history: The ‘Dalmatian horsemen’ hailed from the western Balkans, roughly equivalent to the position of modern-day Croatia. Formed later in the Roman Empire as a temporary adjunct to the Legions, they became known as a ‘vexillationes’ following a reorganisation and expansion of Roman cavalry forces. In the years immediately prior the Legions had taken some heavy losses from the superior horse units of the eastern empires. This reorganisation was almost certainly an attempt to curb Roman losses and enable them to compete with the enemy's burgeoning cavalry tactics. In any case, the Dalmatae were the largest of the newly-raised vexillationes, and contributed to Claudius II victory over the Goths – a worthy record indeed!
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
